en: The Sudhālaharī composed by Paṇḍitarāja Śrī Jagannātha:
An exhilaration for the swarms of bees intoxicated by the clusters of blossoming lotuses; a deliverance for the female ruddy geese whose hearts are distressed by the forest fire of grief.
A portent for those of dark nature, a partiality for eyes whose brilliance is impaired, a certain massing of splendors—this has appeared from the slopes of the mountain of sunrise.

May those rays of the rising sun grant us joy—rays that instantly dissolve the pride of the moonbeams, which, though white and filling the quarters, are hostile to the lotuses; rays that blaze with an abundance of bursting redness;

rays that have undertaken a vow to illuminate the surface of the earth blinded by darkness even from afar; and rays that are expert in destroying wretchedness and overflowing with milk at the dawn of day.

May the rays of the Sun be the adversaries of my sins—those who protect millions afflicted by disease and distress, who perform the daily protection of many gods, who are like wish-fulfilling trees for their devotees, who resemble the brilliance of gold in the shimmering flames, whose initiation (*īkṣā*) brings welfare to the world, who bestow the fortune of *lākṣā* upon the lotus-assemblies [of the sages], and who are expert in destroying the wicked. // JSudh_3 //

May the expansive garlands of rays from the sun bring you auspiciousness as they pervade the sky—garlands that are formidable against the frost, which have swallowed the masses of darkness over the circle of the earth; which have bathed the guardians of the celestial realms; which cast off their young sprouts of crimson light as they burst forth; and which are matted with the nets of your fame that arise to dispel the fever of the young female cakravāka birds as they separate from their mates.

May those rays of the Sun protect you—rays by which, having pierced through the exceedingly dense interior of trees and entered the earth, people set their feet down with minds filled with the illusion that they are holding long golden staffs; and by which, when the tips of leaves are shattered so that shimmering particles of frost fall away, young parrots move their beaks with the thought that they are seeds of the pomegranate.

May the hands of the Sun-god, skilled in arranging the worship of Śrī, protect us—hands that at daybreak swiftly fling open the doors of the lotus-palaces accustomed to sporting by day, and then seal the lily-houses once they have been released; and which, moreover, sprinkle the entire surface of the earth with water infused with crushed saffron.

May the rays of the sun bring us auspiciousness as they travel from afar across the ocean— rays that possess the playful charm of fresh, blossoming sprouts upon the tips of trees on the clear summits of the palaces of kings (which resemble vermilion ointments), yet which appear like masses of acacia charcoal piled atop great heaps of snow.
This entire web of the world has been drenched with the liquid of saffron; pearls have been released from the prison-interiors of lotuses torn open by intoxicated bees;
a thousand cows have been set free, and the loud clamor of the twice-born is heard; and by the good fortune of the gods, a jewel of a son is born to the quarter of Indra.

May that radiance of the Sun never depart from the path of our vision—she who gives birth day after day to the playful manifestations of consciousness within all beings; she who, arriving in the evening, swiftly withdraws them back into the womb of the ocean; and she who exceedingly increases the wealth of the exquisite beauty of the multitude of jewels upon the mountain of gems.

Having observed from afar that the night has brought about the destruction of the lotuses by its dense masses of darkness, as well as the destruction of the eyes and even the performance of Vedic and Smṛti rites,
may the radiance of the sharp-rayed sun, arriving with a speed exceeding that of the ocean from its vicinity, swiftly and utterly sever all the bonds of our desires toward the quarter of Indra.
Alleviating the sorrow of the cold, causing the moon’s light to wane, swiftly destroying the night, censuring the mass of darkness, and bringing forth dejection in the assembly of night-lotuses;

displaying wisdom in the day-lotuses, daily increasing its splendor in the quarters, and spreading across the sky at dawn—may the Sun, who is worshipped by the whole world, ever follow after us out of compassion.

May that jewel of the sky protect you with constant bliss—He who has arrived from the direction of Indra, instantly dispelling the sleep of those overcome by slumber, the disease of those with ailments, the darkness of the three worlds, and the sin of those defiled by evil; He whose playful act of departing forever is a jest to the lotus-ponds, whose nature is the protection of the world from suffering, and who is the very dharma of refuge for all.
May the rays of the Sun, which daily reflect within the waters of the rivers all around the earth— showing it as thick with clusters of rising jewels from the Mountain of the Gods—
and which appear like a mass of rubies in the midst of the sky amidst the spray of water-drops from the *añjali* offerings cast upward by Brahmins at twilight, uproot my languor.

May that Blessed One, the Beloved of the Lotus, bestow upon you steadfastness— He upon whose crest the setting mountain bears the grace of a jeweled parasol, while assemblies of bold young women whose husbands have gone abroad cast up their eyes with fear, with hope, and with mature compassion.

Salutations to that certain supreme deity among the great sages (paramahaṃsa), to whom the priests of the earth offer their twilight salutations with joined palms at both evening and morning; he who, having swiftly dispelled the vast darkness between heaven and earth, reddens it as if with the blood of his own [enemies] won in victory. JSudh_15 //

May that light of the sharp-rayed sun protect us—the refuge of the gods, the crossing for those whose bodies are exhausted by the heat of the waters, the inconceivable end of the rivers, and the fourth state of the three qualities;
which, by its power, brings an end to such a mass of exceedingly thick darkness and possesses the skill to turn the three worlds copper-red with its brilliance.

The playful movements of the Lord of Cows (Kṛṣṇa), who delights in the cows, are like the sun; they are sung with thousands of verses overflowing with praise for his multitude of virtues by the Gandharvas, who sing songs with voices reaching the heights of heaven, and by the leaders of the gods, as they immerse themselves again and again in the rows of houses of those who lament in their helplessness, dispelling the pain of disease and swallowing the village of ailments.

May that light— the life-sustainer for those afflicted by the ailments born of the dense web of dullness, possessing the luster of molten gold, swift as the legs of couriers, expanding upon the earth from the womb of the ocean,
the source of life for all people, the progenitor of splendor, and the blazing radiance of the sun and the moon— arise for your victory.

May those rays of the Lord of Day, whose auspicious form is composed of bliss, extend security to you—rays which, having emerged at dawn and wandered through the realm of light with the cows, hasten again toward their assembly in the evening along with them; rays whose divine power is the sole forest fire that burns the rows of the forest of sins in the three worlds.

May this orb of the rising sun on the mountain of sunrise dispel primordial ignorance— this orb which, at the end of the night, incessantly bestows heart-pleasing knowledge upon hosts of gods, upon the sons of Danu, upon the Rakshasas, and upon the Gandharvas led by their chiefs, as well as upon the Kinnaras and men who bow before the foremost of sages, while illuminating the heavens with its radiance.

The ancient masters, who are experts in the Purāṇas and Āgamas, declare that the wheel of time consists of moments, instants, ghaṭikās, and so forth, which is the playful manifestation of whose sport constitutes the sixfold transformations of all beings through their various states. That fierce-rayed sun, who thus perpetually brings these forth, now shines at dawn within the radiant orb of Indra’s eastern quarter.

May the rays of the sun, the destroyer of sins, swiftly remove my consumption—a disease that has ravaged my entire lineage, which was arrogant in its destruction of Dharma—rays that are crimson as if out of wrath toward enemies, falling suddenly from the eastern quarter like limbs of Brahmins shattered by contact with the weight of frost at dawn; and may they beautify the earth. (JSudh 22)

May that Lord of Days, moist with compassion, who desires to grant rest to the Brahmins, exceeding happiness to those possessed by desire, the steady playfulness to the lotuses, and awakening to the assemblies of night-lilies—
having cast the entire burden of men into the fire within the ocean— be for your great welfare.
May those rays of the sun, which at dawn swiftly strike and dispel the moonlight of the Himalayan night, and out of curiosity once again restore it in the evening with rising and mature compassion;
and which, at dawn, [awaken] the shoots of the Aruṇa flowers and the rows of Indra’s beetles—may those rays of the sun uproot the exhaustion of you whose feet are heavy [with merit].

May the orb of the sun, kissing the peak of the Eastern Mountain, swiftly spread non-duality throughout the three worlds; may it dispel the lethargy of the wives of the Cakravāka birds with its saffron-hued splendors, and may it wash away the darkness within my own heart with its most expansive rays, drawing it forth from the ocean of blindness blinded by sloth.

May that glorious Sun-Kalpa-tree grant you your desired objects forever: he whose pure Brahman is the basin for irrigation, whose root is Nature (Prakṛti), whose trunk is the Supreme Self, whose golden branches are his rays, whose play is the blossoming redness of his sprouts, whose blue sky is the swarm of bees, and who bears the burden of fruits that are the four goals of life—Dharma, Artha, Kāma, and Mokṣa.
May those rays of the sun— who at dawn constantly dispel the mist from the rivers, sleep from the eyes of all lotuses, and the flocks of birds from their nests—
and who at evening again provide them with shelter out of compassion— may they, exerting themselves with intense pity, be able to destroy your exhaustion.

May those rays of the Sun—delightful as gold, dispelling the heart's disease through their desire for our welfare—bring us joy; for they daily enter without hesitation the interiors of houses through rows of openings, wishing to instantly remove the mass of darkness both outside and within, while gladdening the senses of all embodied beings and stealing away the chill of winter.
Adorning the universe while circling in the sky in rings around the eggs of Brahmā, punishing the heretics born of the sons of Danu, and beautifying the quarters of Indra;

may those rays of the fierce-rayed sun—possessing formidable wisdom for the purpose of shattering the fragments of the *pauṇḍarīka* lotuses—swiftly here dispel my paleness, being themselves free from cruelty.
The Vedas proclaimed that he stands above all rows of sins; indeed, they brought the lotus to serve as his seat for the sake of accompanying his eyes.
His lips are the Ṛg and Sāman; may this very Lord of the Day—the Inner Self of all, whose beard and hair are like molten gold, and whose entire body is [radiant]—grant you supreme auspiciousness.
Thus ends the *Sudhālaharī*, composed by Paṇḍitarāja Śrī Jagannātha.
